alt: Two strict-rule cases: Cutter v Powell, where a sailor’s widow recovered nothing because the voyage was not completed, and Re Moore and Landauer, where wrongly packed tins could be rejected. Below, bars show Hoenig v Isaacs, where the price was payable less the cost of defects of about £56 on a £750 contract, and Bolton v Mahadeva, where serious defects meant nothing was payable.
caption: The strict rule is harsh; substantial performance earns the price less the cost of repairs.

alt: Four further exceptions. Severable contracts: payment for each completed stage. Acceptance of partial performance: only with a genuine choice to accept (Sumpter v Hedges). Prevented performance: a reasonable sum on a quantum meruit (Planché v Colburn). Tender of performance: a wrongly refused offer to perform counts (Startup v Macdonald).
caption: Stages, genuine acceptance, prevention and tender can all earn payment.

alt: Actual breach happens when performance is due; anticipatory breach before it is due. A repudiatory breach, meaning breach of a condition, a serious breach of an innominate term or a refusal to perform, lets the innocent party choose to terminate and claim damages or affirm and continue. A minor breach gives damages only.
caption: A repudiatory breach gives a choice: terminate or affirm. A minor one gives damages only.

alt: A timeline from contract to repudiation to the date performance is due. In Hochster v De la Tour the courier was told in May he would not be needed from 1 June. Option 1: accept the repudiation and sue at once, with damages assessed by reference to the performance date and a duty to mitigate (Hochster; Frost v Knight). Option 2: affirm and wait, as in White and Carter v McGregor, but at the risk shown in Avery v Bowden, where war frustrated the contract and the claim was lost.
caption: Accepting lets you sue at once; affirming keeps the contract alive for both sides.

alt: Five categories of frustration with cases: destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell), death or incapacity in a personal contract (Robinson v Davison; Condor v Baron Knights), supervening illegality (Metropolitan Water Board v Dick Kerr), purpose defeated (Krell v Henry) and long interruption (Jackson v Union Marine Insurance). The test from Davis Contractors is performance radically different from what was undertaken.
caption: An event after formation, without fault, that makes performance radically different.

alt: Bars show Davis Contractors, where a job planned for 8 months took 22 and cost more but was not frustrated. Four further limits: harder or dearer is not enough (Tsakiroglou); the purpose must be wholly defeated (Herne Bay Steam Boat v Hutton, contrasted with Krell v Henry); self-induced frustration does not count (Maritime National Fish; The Super Servant Two); and an express clause such as force majeure governs instead.
caption: More time, more cost or a partly defeated purpose is not frustration.

alt: The Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943. Section 1(2): money paid before frustration is recoverable and money payable ceases to be payable, but the court may allow the payee expenses up to that amount. Section 1(3): a party who received a valuable non-money benefit may be ordered to pay a just sum (BP Exploration v Hunt).
caption: Money comes back, less allowed expenses; other benefits are paid for with a just sum.

alt: Dana’s case: the April refusal is an anticipatory breach; she affirms, keeping the contract alive; the 18 June ban on events likely frustrates it; so, as in Avery v Bowden, her claim for the earlier breach is lost; under section 1(2) of the 1943 Act she recovers her £1,000 deposit less any expenses the court allows.
caption: Affirming an anticipatory breach can backfire if the contract is then frustrated.
